A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Sylber and contain readable text, equations, figures, tables and appendices. Corresponding methods and experiments can be matched reliably despite substantial reorganization and additions.

before.justification: v1 reports original syllable detection, resynthesis, coding-efficiency, language-modeling and categorical-perception results, plus appendix ablations and SUPERB evaluations.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds multilingual and conversational-speech evaluations, human ratings, larger-corpus language-model experiments, initialization ablations and runtime measurements.

M1.justification: v1 uses an EMA teacher; v2 specifies a teacher frozen within each training stage and replaced between stages (Section 3.1 and Appendix A.1.5). Algorithm 1 also changes frame-to-frame similarity to similarity against the running segment mean and adds neighboring-segment merging during refinement. These alter the reported training and inference procedures.

E1.justification: v2 adds syllable detection on noisy English conversations from Fisher, Spanish reading from MLS and Mandarin reading from AISHELL-3. It also adds phoneme-boundary detection with supervised initial segments, distinct from the retained phoneme-recognition task. Articulatory-codec training is described using LibriTTS-R rather than v1's LibriTTS-R/LibriTTS/EXPRESSO mixture.

E2.justification: v2 Table 6 adds NAST and TWIST, including cold-initialized and 13B variants, to the existing language-model comparisons. Table 1 adds Sylber-MinCut, HuBERT-Greedy and SDHuBERT-Greedy comparisons. These substantially broaden both competitive baselines and comparisons separating representation quality from segmentation algorithm.

E3.justification: Reported Sylber training budgets change from 1.15M/500K to 115K/50K updates, and low-amplitude filtering changes from 0.05 to 0.1. New settings include 66K-hour uLM training, HuBERT resynthesis with 500/2K clusters, subjective naturalness/prosody metrics and controlled runtime tests. The revised settings do not establish that numerically retained results were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond retained training-stage, denoising, threshold and SUPERB analyses, v2 adds model/segmenter swaps, cross-domain robustness, noisy-boundary and weight-initialization ablations, phoneme-initialized training, embedding visualizations and input-length analyses (Table 1 and Appendices A.2.5-A.2.9). These address previously untested questions about initialization dependence, representation structure and generalization.

E5.justification: Both versions report 95% confidence intervals for reconstruction and UTMOS results, with the same practice extended to additional resynthesis rows. No new repeated-run, seed or significance-testing protocol is specified. The added human-rating results report point estimates without uncertainty.

E6.justification: Most previous tabulated scores remain numerically unchanged, including syllable F1 of 72.2 and overall DI of 0.112. Substantial new results include OOD F1 scores of 71.9/71.7/71.3 for Fisher/Spanish/Mandarin, 66K-hour uLM scores of 76.31/60.54 and silence-variant scores of 78.03/60.78 for sWUGGY/sBLIMP, human ratings, initialization results and measured runtime. Larger-corpus results are new-setting results, not same-setting gains over v1.

T1.justification: Appendix A.1.1 changes the formal segment-assignment condition from s_j,0 <= i < s_j,1 to s_j,0 <= i <= s_j,1, making the endpoint inclusive. The distillation loss and Discriminability Index definition otherwise remain unchanged; the latter moves into the appendix. No new theorem or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: v2 makes generalization to noisy conversational speech and unseen Spanish/Mandarin an explicit abstract and introduction contribution, substantially broadening the claimed applicability. It also qualifies language-model superiority as comparable or better performance under similar resources. The central syllabic-tokenization, linear-time segmentation and categorical-perception claims remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations linking multilingual transfer to shared phonology, embedding clusters to phonological similarity and input-length stability to information carried by tokens. It explains when HuBERT initialization suffices and notes collapse when training from scratch. The SUPERB limitation remains, but v1's explicit limitation about unscaled Sylber training is dropped even though the newly scaled experiments concern uLMs.

D1.justification: v2 substantially expands reproducibility information: GPU hardware, uLM token crops and LibriLight splits, segmentation boundary-offset calibration, 16,384-to-4,096 clustering, and OOD alignment and syllabification procedures. Several retained-experiment details are newly disclosed rather than demonstrated setting changes. Training budgets and filtering parameters are also revised; code/audio links and release promises remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 adds NAST, corpus/alignment references and Ohala's phonological accounts, while removing the Grill, Caron and He citations supporting EMA distillation. The main related-work narrative around SSL tokenization and prior syllable discovery remains intact. Articulatory Encodec/SPARC refers to the updated Cho et al. work, rather than a newly introduced cited method.

P1.justification: Categorical-perception setup and findings are consolidated into later Section 6, while its formal definition and several segmentation/resynthesis details move into the appendix. The appendix is reorganized into implementation details and additional analyses. The abstract, conclusion and substantial explanatory passages are also rewritten, producing a materially different narrative structure.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn and compacted, Figure 2 gains a similarity color scale, and the uLM table expands into a resource-aware comparison. New tables display OOD detection, human ratings, initialization experiments and runtime; Figures 5-9 add generalization examples, ablation matrices, embedding plots, length-dependent results and alignments. Existing displays are also relocated and reformatted.

improvement.justification: The added OOD tests, algorithm/initialization ablations, measured runtime and larger-corpus uLM experiments resolve substantial gaps in validation of robustness, practical efficiency and scalability. Expanded implementation details make the evidence easier to assess and reproduce. Human-rating procedures remain underspecified, and Table 6 lists tGSLM training as 6K hours while Section 5.3 says 150K, but these shortcomings do not outweigh the substantial targeted validation.
